oscarqht/pikmin-rush-by-opus-5.5.readme:
# Bulborb Rush: A Pikmin Tower Defense (React Edition)

A Kingdom Rush–style tower defense game set in the world of Pikmin, with the roles reversed. You command the native creatures (Bulborbs, Breadbugs, Blowhogs, Groinks, Cannon Beetles and more). The Pikmin and their captains (Olimar, Louie, Alph, Brittany, Charlie and the President) are the invaders.

All art and audio are generated procedurally at runtime with Canvas 2D vector drawing and Web Audio synthesis. The application is built with React, TypeScript, and Vite.

## Screenshots

**Tranquil Grove.** A Pikmin column marches in from the Onion while Groinks, Blowhogs, Cannon Beetles and Bulborb dens hold the trail.

![Gameplay: Tranquil Grove](screenshots/03-gameplay-grove.png)

**Twilight Hollow.** The night finale, with Glow Pikmin, fireflies, glowing mushrooms and the President's boss bar.

![Gameplay: Twilight Hollow boss wave](screenshots/06-gameplay-twilight-boss.png)

| Title screen | World map |
| --- | --- |
| ![Title](screenshots/01-title.png) | ![World map](screenshots/02-world-map.png) |
| **Awakening Wood** | **Perplexing Pool** |
| ![Awakening Wood](screenshots/04-gameplay-wood.png) | ![Perplexing Pool](screenshots/05-gameplay-pool.png) |

## Development & Run

This project runs on Node.js with Vite:

```bash
# Install dependencies
npm install

# Run the development server (port 3000)
npm run dev

# Build for production
npm run build
```

## Features

- **React Architecture**: Modular components for screens (Title, World Map, Game canvas view) and modals (Briefing, Piklopedia Almanac, Pause, Results, and About).
- **Procedural Canvas 2D Engine**: All creatures, animations, environments, shadows, effects, and map geography are procedurally rendered without external image files.
- **Synthesized Audio Engine**: Real-time generative chiptune music for themes (Title, Map, Meadow, Forest, Pool, Twilight) and procedural sound effects via Web Audio API.
- **4 Levels**:
  - Tranquil Grove (Meadow)
  - Awakening Wood (Autumn Forest, dual trails)
  - Perplexing Pool (Water ponds, Koppaites)
  - Twilight Hollow (Night, Glow Pikmin, President boss battle)
- **Towers & Upgrades**: 4 tower families (Gatling Groink, Bulborb Den, Fiery Blowhog, Cannon Beetle Larva) with 3 tiers and elite tier-4 specializations.
- **Emperor Bulblax Hero**: Moveable hero unit with ground stomps, group tongue attacks, leveling, and respawns.
- **Special Spells**: Snagret Strike (summoning Burrowing Snagret) and Bulborb Reinforcements.
- **Piklopedia (Almanac)**: Interactive compendium with live animated previews and complete creature/invader combat statistics.
- **Persistent Progress**: Star ratings, difficulty selection, and seen invaders saved in localStorage.

oscarqht/pikmin-rush-by-gemini-4.readme:
# PNF-404 Rush: Native Defense

A **Kingdom Rush**-inspired Tower Defense web game set on planet **PNF-404**, where you command native PNF-404 wildlife (**Bulborbs**, **Burrowing Snagrets**, **Fiery Blowhogs**, **Armored Cannon Beetles**, and **Breadbugs**) to defend the planet's Sparklium Core against waves of invading **Pikmin** and **Hocotate/Koppai Captains**.

Built with zero external dependencies using vanilla JavaScript, HTML5 Canvas, procedural vector sprites, and a Web Audio API sound synthesizer.

---

## Screenshots

### Live Gameplay
![Live Gameplay - PNF-404 Rush](screenshots/gameplay_battle.png)

### Procedural Tower & Enemy Roster (`showcase.html`)
![Tower & Enemy Sprite Roster](screenshots/sprite_showcase.png)

### Interactive Piklopedia Field Guide
![Piklopedia Field Guide](screenshots/piklopedia.png)

---

## Features

- **Kingdom Rush Tactical Mechanics**:
  - **Barracks & Rally Points**: Deploy Dwarf Bulborb packs and Breadbug Scavengers directly onto the lane to intercept and block marching Pikmin squads.
  - **Lv. 1–3 Upgrades + Lv. 4 Branching Specializations**: Every tower line splits into two distinct Lv. 4 specializations with custom abilities.
  - **Commandable Heroes**: Switch between **Empress Bulblax** (tanky lane crusher with shockwave & larva spawns) and **Titan Dweevil** (ranged elemental AoE caster) and click anywhere on the map to move them.
  - **Global Spells**: Call down **Falling Boulders** (meteor AoE + stun) or summon a **Sheargrub Swarm** anywhere on the road.
  - **Early Wave Call**: Click pulsing skull wave indicators or the Next Wave button early for bonus Sparklium.

### Native Defender Towers
| Tower | Role | Lv. 4 Branch A | Lv. 4 Branch B |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Bulborb Den** | Melee Barracks (3 Blockers) | **Emperor Bulblax** (Tongue Slurp instakill + Roar stun) | **Fiery Bulblax** (Ignites attackers, immune to fire) |
| **Snagret Burrow** | Ranged Physical Marksman | **Pileated Snagret** (Crit peck + armor shred) | **Burrowing Snagret Trio** (3-target rapid barrage) |
| **Blowhog Vent** | Elemental Breath (Ignores Armor) | **Withering Blowhog** ( strips flowers + +40% damage vulnerability) | **Watery / Electric Blowhog** (Chain lightning + stun puddle) |
| **Cannon Beetle** | Heavy AoE Boulder Artillery | **Horned Cannon Beetle** (Homing magnetic boulders) | **Groovy Long Legs** (Disco AoE slow/confuse + rhythm stomp) |
| **Breadbug Nest** | Trap / Scavenger Support | **Giant Breadbug** (Drags medium enemies & captains backward, +Sparklium) | **Joustmite Nest** (Armored ambush piercer + bleed) |

### Invading Pikmin & Captains
- **Pikmin Types**: Red (fire-resistant), Yellow (electric-immune, fast), Blue (water-immune), Purple (heavy armor, 2-blocker weight), White (acid trail on death, poison-immune, sprints), Winged (flying over ground blockers), Rock (60% physical armor, immune to boulder crush), Ice (chills attackers on hit), Glow (teleports past first blocker).
- **Maturity Ranks**: Leaf (1.0× speed), Bud (1.2× speed), and **Flower** (1.45× speed — can be stripped back to Leaf by the **Withering Blowhog**).
- **Bosses & Captains**: Captain Olimar (whistle heal + speed aura), Louie (King Beady Long Legs mount), Alph & Brittany (Rock/Winged squad), Oatchi (rush charge), and the **Ancient Sirehound** (multi-phase elemental titan).

---

## Running Locally

Open `index.html` directly in any modern browser, or serve the directory with a local static server:

```bash
python3 -m http.server 8080
```

- **Main Game**: `http://localhost:8080/index.html`
- **Sprite & Evolution Sheet**: `http://localhost:8080/showcase.html`
- **Verification Script**: `node check.js`

danieldownes/PizzaWorm.readme:
# Pizza Worm — in the browser I'm a big fan of **Pizza Worm**, a 1995 DOS freeware game by Sami "Zorlim" Lehtinen (graphics by AOK, music by Izzard). This repository is pure retro nostalgia: a faithful re-implementation of version 2.1G that runs in a web browser, built by taking the original `PWORM.EXE` apart and porting its logic routine by routine.

**Play it** in the browser with the button above, or download [`index.html`](index.html) and open it locally. It is one self-contained file and works offline. | Player 1 (green) | Player 2 (red) | Anywhere | |---|---|---| | `←` `→` steer | `Z` `C` steer | `P` pause, `Esc` end round, `S` sound on/off | On the score screen press `1` or `2` for a one- or two-player game. On a phone, hold the left or right half of the screen to steer and tap to confirm. The original game said *"THIS PROGRAM IS SO CALLED FREEWARE, SO SPREAD THIS!"* — the untouched original release is kept in [`pworm21g.zip`](pworm21g.zip), with the author's own `PWORM.DOC`. All credit for the game, its art and its music belongs to its creators. --- ## Repository layout ``` pworm21g.zip original 2.1G release archive (runs in DOSBox) index.html the playable browser version (generated, ~420 KB) src/ game.js the game, ported from the EXE modplayer.js small ProTracker replayer + sound-effect channel page.html page shell, renderer, input and audio glue build.py embeds the original data files (read from the zip) and writes index.html ``` Rebuild with `python src/build.py`. ## What was in the box | File | What it turned out to be | |---|---| | `PWORM.EXE` | Turbo Pascal 7 program (MZ, not packed), with the MIDAS Sound System 0.4 linked in | | `PWORM.001` | A 4-channel ProTracker `M.K.` module, *"Pizza Worm -Izzard-"*. Instruments 1–9 are the voice clips (`argh`, `laugh`, `c00l`, `sika`, `jam`, `good`, `namnam`, `I am hungry`…) | | `PWORM.002` | 320×200×256 PCX: high-score screen | | `PWORM.003` | 320×200×256 PCX: Zorlim's pizza parlor (the play field) | | `PWORM.004` | 320×200×256 PCX: title picture | | `PWORM.000` | High-score table (10 × name, score, checksum byte, plus a file checksum) | | `PWORM.DOC` | The author's docs and version history | The copy of `PWORM.000` here is all zeros, which the game treats as tampering ("LAMER! WARNING!"). The browser version keeps its own table in `localStorage`. ## How the decompilation was done 1. **Loading the image.** The MZ header gives a 6304-byte header and 1567 relocations. Reading the relocated words yields the list of segments: the main program at `0000`, a dozen units (graphics, file loading, keyboard, MIDAS wrappers, timer) and the Turbo Pascal `System` unit at `11A5`. The data segment is `1392`. 2. **Recursive-descent disassembly** with Capstone (16-bit x86), seeded from the entry point and every far-call relocation. Turbo Pascal puts string constants right in front of the procedure that uses them, so the undecoded gaps between procedures read as Pascal strings (`PAUSE`, `Player one won last round`, the parameter help…). This gave ~70 procedures in the main program. 3. **Identifying the runtime.** The 6-byte `Real` routines in `System` were matched by behaviour: `13C4` add, `13CA` subtract, `13D0` square, `13D6` multiply, `13DC` divide, `13EA` integer→real, `13EE` Trunc and `13F6` Round (the same helper with a rounding flag). `150F`/`14FC` are Sin/Cos, `149D` Sqrt, `1883` Random. Real48 constants were decoded by hand from the register loads, e.g. `80 2D 33 F3 04 35` = 0.7071 (1/√2), `86 E9 D2 E0 2E 65` = 57.2958 (degrees per radian). 4. **Naming the globals.** Variables were identified by how they are used, e.g. `

danieldownes/AtomicBomberman.readme:
# Atomic Bomberman: HTML5 port

[![Play in your browser](https://img.shields.io/badge/%E2%96%B6%20Play-in%20your%20browser-f8d848?style=for-the-badge)](https://danieldownes.github.io/AtomicBomberman/)
A browser version of Interplay/Hudson Soft's *Atomic Bomberman* (1997). It is rebuilt from the
original CD: the graphics, sounds, music, arenas, schemes and tuning tables are the game's own,
and the game logic follows the decompiled executable. It runs in any current browser, from GitHub
Pages or straight from disk.

Besides the original game, the port adds:

* **Campaign Mode:** the original's hidden single-player campaign, with ghosts and rovers.
* **Sounds & Voices browser:** every recording on the CD, including about 1,050 the game never
  used, grouped by event and phrase.
* **Child-friendly and uncensored voice presets.**
* **Idle animations** that were cut from the original.
* **An extra 8-bit "Classic" arena.**
* **The CD's intro movie.**

## Play

* **Online:** use the button above.
* **Locally:** open `web/index.html` in Chrome, Edge or Firefox. No server is needed.

The first load downloads about 4 MB, and each round loads its sounds (about 4 MB). Both show a
progress bar.

## What's in the repository

```
web/          the game (see web/README.md for controls, options and how it works)
tools/        the scripts that convert the CD into web/ (see tools/README.md)
decompiled/   pseudo-C of BM95.EXE, used as the reference for the game logic
```

The CD image and the files extracted from it are not included. To rebuild `web/`, put your own
copy of the CD in this folder and follow `tools/README.md`.

## Credits

*Atomic Bomberman* is © 1997 Interplay Productions and Hudson Soft. Bomberman is a trademark of
Hudson Soft (now Konami). This is an unofficial fan project, and all game content belongs to its
owners.

ericvaladas/azragon.readme:
# AZRAGON

You are a skyscraper-sized alien that has crash-landed on Earth. Flatten the city while the military throws everything it has at you.

## Controls

| Action | Phone | Desktop |
|---|---|---|
| Walk | Tap ground | Click ground |
| Attack | Tap tank, jet, or building | Click it |
| Orbit camera | Drag | Drag (left or right button) |
| Zoom | — | Mouse wheel |
| Leap | Tap Leap button, then tap a spot | Space, then click |
| Dash (level-up pick) | Tap Dash button (charges straight ahead) | E |
| Roar (level-up pick) | Tap Roar button | R |

## Threats

| Enemy | Arrives at | How to counter it |
|---|---|---|
| Tanks | Level 1 | Stomp them, or spike them from range |
| Jets | Level 2 | Spikes only; they loop back for more passes |
| Kamikaze blimp | Level 3 | Shoot it down before it drifts into your head; Roar knocks it out of the sky |
| SAM silo | Level 5 | Reach it while it's raised; spikes shoot its missiles down |
| Artillery | Level 7 | Step or Leap out of the red circles, or hunt the guns down in the fog |
| Laser cannon truck | Level 9 | Step out of its red sight line once it locks, kill it, or take Overload to fire the beam back |
| Orbital laser | Level 11 | Walk out of the faint beam before it locks, or Leap |

Difficulty follows your level: each level adds enemy toughness and spawn rate. Level-ups offer stat boosts and rankable abilities (Dash, Roar, Spine Shield, Venom Nova, Acid Mortar, Shield Bubble, Reflect Shield, Acid Footprints, Spike Storm, Chitin Deflection, Feeding Frenzy, Brood Swarm, Overload, and more).

## Develop

```bash
npm install
npm run dev       # http://localhost:5173 (?debug=1 for fps/draw calls)
npm test          # unit tests
npm run shot      # phone + desktop screenshots into ./screenshots (dev server must be running)
npm run build
```

All tunable values (look, camera, balance) live in `src/config.ts`.

## Deploy

```bash
rundot login
npm run build && rundot deploy
```

Design spec: `docs/superpowers/specs/`. Implementation plan: `docs/superpowers/plans/`.

antxiko/GameMaster2-disassembly.desc: Konami's Game Master 2 (MSX, RC-755): a commented disassembly, with its screens drawn from the ROM and its music
antxiko/GameMaster2-disassembly.readme:
# Konami's Game Master 2 (RC-755) — a commented disassembly

*(También en [castellano](README.es.md).)*

**[→ Read it on the web](https://antxiko.github.io/GameMaster2-disassembly/)**

A complete, commented disassembly of Konami's Game Master 2 for the MSX
(1987), in Japan *Konami no Shin 10-bai Cartridge*: RC-755, 128 KB with SRAM.

It is Konami's **cheat cartridge**: it goes in next to a game, recognises it,
gets into its interrupt and lets you change the stage and the lives, save
screens and games to disk or to its SRAM, and keep a ranking. On its own it has
its own menu: the SRAM utility, a two-player Tennis and Hockey and a
biorhythm.

| | |
|---|---|
| binary explained | **100%**, 131,072 of 131,072 bytes |
| code traced | 36,633 bytes |
| data identified | 94,439 bytes |
| routines | 2,338, **none under-commented** |
| comment density | **40.1%** |
| games it recognises | 30 (68 signatures) |
| screens drawn | 24, checked to 0 |
| tunes | 9, checked against openMSX |
| tests | 14 |

## How it gets in

It looks in the first 256 bytes of the game's start-up code for the address
of an interrupt hook: first H.TIMI (the one Konami's MSX2 cartridges use), then
H.KEYI (the MSX one). That is how it also gets into Vampire Killer and
Hinotori, which Game Master 1 could not do.

## Reproducing it

The cartridge is not distributed. Put your copy in the root as
`gamemaster2.rom` (sha256 `2054636a6ca2…`) and:

    make verify    # reassembles the 16 banks and compares them byte for byte
    make sanity    # checks the trace
    make web       # builds the website

## The pictures and the music

No picture is a capture: they are drawn by reading the cartridge's tables and
checked byte for byte against the running cartridge or the openMSX VRAM. The
tunes come from running its own sound engine and match openMSX frame by frame.

See [LEGAL-NOTICE.md](LEGAL-NOTICE.md) and [LICENSE](LICENSE).

g8r-b8/frontierLab.readme:
# Frontier

**Found an AI lab. Race to AGI. Try not to repeat history.**
**[Play in your browser →](https://g8r-b8.github.io/frontierLab/)**

![The Frontier board](assets/screenshot-board.png)

A Democracy-style management sim about founding a frontier AI lab. It has the same structure as
Positech's *Democracy*: policies on sliders, a web of lagged cause and effect, stakeholder
"voter groups", situations and dilemmas. The difference is that you're racing to AGI instead of
running a country, and history keeps repeating on you.

## Play

Play online at https://g8r-b8.github.io/frontierLab/, or locally:

```sh
open index.html          # just play (no build step, autosaves locally)
npm start                # or: serve at http://localhost:4747 with the terminal bridge
./frontier help          # drive the open game from a terminal (needs npm start)
```

Ask Claude Code to be your chief of staff while you play. `CLAUDE.md` tells it how to read the
live game through `./frontier status --json`, explain what's driving things, and post advice
into the game's advisor panel with `./frontier say`.

## What's in it

| Democracy            | Frontier                                                             |
|----------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Political capital    | Bandwidth (leadership attention)                                     |
| Policies & sliders   | 44 policies in 7 categories (incl. Marketing)                        |
| Simulation values    | 16 stats + 4 indicators, all wired together with lags                |
| Voter groups         | 10 stakeholders (board, investors, researchers, regulators, ...)     |
| Elections            | Funding rounds every 6 quarters, plus dilution                       |
| Assassination        | Board coup                                                           |
| Situations           | 13 situations (talent exodus, injunctions, viral moments, ...)       |
| Dilemmas             | 32 events incl. real AI bloopers, plus a launch-day call per model   |
| Cabinet              | Hiring: named candidates, hiring managers, practices, culture values |
| —                    | GPU fleet: chip generations, failures, depreciation, power, deals    |
| —                    | 18 historical pitfalls across short, medium and long horizons         |
| —                    | 171 verified real quotes/artifacts on the loading screen, in the newspaper and in the Archive; 78 achievements |
| —                    | Marketing: brand vs hype, campaigns (Super Bowl in Q1 only), launch strategy |
| —                    | Multiplayer: real-time, peer to peer, friends + AI labs, chat        |
| —                    | Plague Inc-style growth map; world events hitting all, some or random labs |
| —                    | Cookie Clicker-style golden opportunities, buffs, Legacy prestige perks, joke ticker |
| —                    | Rival moves: poach, price war, espionage, smears, pacts, licensing, acquisitions — and rivals that do it to you |
| —                    | Startup scorecard: Blitzscaling stages, YC weekly growth bar, PMF, burn multiple, default alive |
| —                    | Growth Playbook: commit to Blitzscaling rules or YC maxims (embrace chaos, founder mode, talk to users...) |

It runs in **real time**: the clock never stops for you, decisions expire, and you never see the
whole picture. Rivals are estimates, your own safety is an eval estimate, and every run has a hidden
world with its own rules. There are three difficulties: **Easy**, **Normal** and **Realistic**.

![Quarterly report with a real quote](assets/screenshot-report.png)

Real people and events appear only as sourced archive cards and history notes on pitfalls.
The verified research lives in `tools/research/`. The labs, chips and providers you meet in
play are fictional.

## Layout

- `js/data/*.js`: content and tuning. `archive.js` and `achievements.js` are generated by
  `python3 too

hardwaremack-prog/ember-valley.desc: First-person 3D browser game tuned for the AMD Ryzen AI Max+ 395: gather 12 embers across a procedurally carved valley before sunset.
hardwaremack-prog/ember-valley.readme:
# Ember Valley

![Ember Valley](screenshot.png)

A first-person 3D browser game built to push the **AMD Ryzen AI Max+ 395** (Strix Halo) — 16 Zen 5 cores, Radeon 8060S graphics and a large pool of shared memory.

Twelve embers are scattered across a mountain valley at golden hour. Gather all of them before the sun sets and the valley goes dark.

## Play

Open `index.html` in Chrome or Edge. An internet connection is needed the first time so it can load three.js and the fonts from a CDN.

| Key | Action |
| --- | --- |
| W A S D / arrows | Walk |
| Shift | Run |
| Space | Jump |
| Mouse | Look (click the view to capture the mouse) |
| F | Performance panel |
| M | Sound on/off |
| Esc | Pause |

On a touchscreen, drag the left side to move and the right side to look.

## How it uses the 395

- **Every CPU thread:** each valley is carved in parallel with one Web Worker per thread (up to 32), each working on its own band of terrain rows. The start screen shows a live bar for every thread.
- **Radeon 8060S:** the Strix Ultra preset draws 820,000 GPU-instanced grass blades that read terrain height straight from a texture on the GPU, sway in the wind and glow when backlit. It also renders a 1025 × 1025 terrain (over a million points), thousands of instanced trees and rocks, 4K soft shadows and real-time planar reflections on the lake.
- **Shared memory:** the whole full-detail world stays loaded at once, so there is no streaming or pop-in.
- **Living sky:** a physical sky model drives the lighting, fog and image-based lighting as the sun goes from afternoon to sunset to a starry night.

## Quality presets

| Preset | Terrain | Grass blades | Shadows | Water |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Low | 257² | 90k | 1K | Sky tint |
| High | 513² | 320k | 2K | Reflections |
| Strix Ultra | 1025² | 820k | 4K | Sharp reflections |

The game suggests a preset based on your thread count and GPU.

## Notes

This is a browser game, so it runs on the CPU and GPU through WebGL. It doesn't use the NPU, which browsers can't reach.

# おさかな～のゲーム置き場

静的なゲーム投稿サイト（HTML/CSS/素の JS のみ、外部依存なし）。GitHub Pages でそのまま公開できます。

## 構成
- `index.html` 一覧 / `play.html?id=xxx` プレイ画面（iframe）
- `games.js` ゲームのデータ（ここに追記するだけで一覧に反映）
- `games/` ゲーム本体、`thumbs/` サムネイル
- `terms.html` / `license.html` / `privacy.html` 規約ページ（最終更新日を編集時に更新）

## ゲームの追加手順
1. `games/名前/index.html` にゲームを置く（サムネは `thumbs/` に、16:9 推奨）。
2. `games.js` 冒頭の雛形をコピーして最後に追加。`url` が空なら「準備中」表示。
3. `mode` は `"embed"`（サイト内で表示）か `"external"`（新しいタブ）。

## 公開手順（GitHub Pages）
1. GitHub にリポジトリを作り、このフォルダの内容を push。
2. Settings → Pages → Branch を `master`（/root）にして保存。
3. `https://ユーザー名.github.io/リポジトリ名/` で公開されます（`404.html` は直下のみ想定）。

Radomir-Aksenenko/code_to_redstone.desc: Compiler from logic (RSL or node graph) to verified Minecraft redstone builds: .schem, .litematic, .mcfunction
Radomir-Aksenenko/code_to_redstone.readme:
# code_to_redstone

Компилятор логики в редстоун для Minecraft Java. Вы описываете схему кодом или графом узлов, на выходе получаете постройку (`.schem`, `.litematic`, `.mcfunction`), проверенную в тиковом симуляторе.

Руками раскладывать пыль, повторители и компараторы не нужно: размещение и трассировка делаются автоматически, а результат сверяется с логической моделью.

## Что внутри

| Модуль | Назначение |
|---|---|
| `packages/core` | Вся логика: блоки, структуры, NBT, экспорт, симулятор, ячейки, HDL, синтез, размещение и трассировка. Работает в Node и в браузере |
| `packages/web` | Редактор графа узлов на React: компиляция, проверка и экспорт прямо в браузере |
| `skill/` | База знаний по редстоуну для Claude: справочники и чертежи |
| `docs/` | Архитектура, заметки из игры, отчёт поиска вентилей |

## Как это устроено

```
RSL / граф узлов
      |
  разбор и elaborate        packages/core/src/hdl
      |
  нетлист и оптимизация     packages/core/src/ir
      |
  подбор ячеек              packages/core/src/techmap, cells
      |
  размещение и трассировка  packages/core/src/pnr
      |
  симулятор, проверка       packages/core/src/sim, verify
      |
  .schem  .litematic  .mcfunction
```

- **Ячейки** (`cells/`): вентили, макро-ячейки (например XOR из двух компараторов) и последовательные элементы в двух режимах: `fast` и `compact`.
- **Маршрутизатор** (`pnr/`): детерминированный канальный, профиль с низкими каналами (ответвления на y=1, магистрали на y=3). Есть плотная укладка `dense.ts` для минимального объёма.
- **Симулятор** (`sim/`): правила Java Edition, тик за тиком. Каждая сгенерированная структура в тестах проходит через него.
- **Шаблоны** (`templates/`): параметрические постройки, фермы, логические блоки и дисплеи.
- **Синтез** (`synth/`): отжиг, который ищет вентили без факелов и повторителей. Результаты в [docs/synth-report.md](docs/synth-report.md).

## Язык RSL

```
module full_adder(in a, in b, in cin, out s, out cout) {
  s = a ^ b ^ cin;
  cout = (a & b) | (cin & (a ^ b));
}

module counter(in clk, in rst, out q[4]) {
  reg r[4] @clk;
  r <= rst ? 0 : r + 1;
  q = r;
}
```

Побитовые операции, редукции, сложение и вычитание, сравнения, сдвиги на константу, тернарный оператор, конкатенация, срезы, регистры по фронту, ПЗУ, циклы `for`. Входы становятся рычагами, выходы лампами. Ошибки указывают строку и столбец. Полная грамматика: [docs/ARCHITECTURE.md](docs/ARCHITECTURE.md), раздел 5.

## Быстрый старт

Нужны Node 24 и npm.

```bash
npm install
```

```bash
npm test
```

```bash
npm run typecheck
```

Веб-редактор:

```bash
npm run dev -w @c2r/web
```

Поиск вентилей без факелов:

```bash
npm run synth -w @c2r/core
```

## Использование как библиотеки

```ts
import { Structure, Simulator, toSchem, toLitematic, toMcfunction, toAsciiLayers } from '@c2r/core';
```

Публичный API экспортируется из [packages/core/src/index.ts](packages/core/src/index.ts). Пакеты помечены `private`, в npm они не публикуются.

## Соглашения

- Оси: +X восток, +Y вверх, +Z юг.
- Для повторителя и компаратора `facing=F` означает: вход в `pos+F`, выход в `pos-F`.
- В `core/src` нет импортов `fs`, `path`, `zlib`, чтобы пакет работал в браузере. Gzip через `fflate`.
- Постройка считается готовой, только если её проверил симулятор.

## Состояние

| Часть | Статус |
|---|---|
| Блоки, структуры, NBT, экспорт `.schem` / `.litematic` / `.mcfunction` | Готово |
| Симулятор | Готово, правила сверены с игрой |
| Ячейки, компиляция RSL, размещение и трассировка | Работает, идёт работа над компактностью |
| Веб-редактор графа | Работает: компиляция, проверка, экспорт |
| Шаблоны построек | Готово |
| MCP-сервер, библиотека готовых модулей (ALU, CPU) | Спроектированы, не реализованы |

Результаты проверки в игре записаны в [docs/ingame-lessons.md](docs/ingame-lessons.md), справочник механик в [docs/redstone-kb.md](docs/redstone-kb.md).

## Документация

- [docs/ARCHITECTURE.md](docs/ARCHITECTURE.md): контракты модулей, маршрутизация, RSL, гр

braxten509/arm32-bridge.desc: Run 32-bit ARM Android games on 64-bit-only phones (Pixel 10): ARM32-to-ARM64 translator with Unicorn fallback
braxten509/arm32-bridge.readme:
> [!NOTE]
> **This project was made with AI.** The code, the docs and this README were written by an AI coding assistant
> (Anthropic's Claude), directed and tested on a real phone by Braxten Chenay. Expect rough edges.

# Game Bridge (arm32-bridge)

Play old 32-bit Android games on new phones that can only run 64-bit apps.

Newer phones like the Pixel 10 have processors without a 32-bit mode, so many older games (made before 2019 or
so) won't install at all ("App not compatible"). Game Bridge converts such a game on the phone itself: it swaps
the game's 32-bit code for a bridge that translates it to 64-bit while the game runs, then installs the result.
The game keeps its own look, sound and save files.

## Download

Get `GameBridge-<version>.apk` from the [Releases page](https://github.com/braxten509/arm32-bridge/releases)
and open it on your phone. No root needed.

**Needs:** a 64-bit ARM Android phone with Android 12 or newer. Only tested on a Pixel 10 with Android 17
(GrapheneOS). If your phone still runs 32-bit apps, you don't need this; install the game normally.

## How to use it

1. Download the game you own as an APK file (or a bundle: `.xapk`, `.apkm`, `.apks`) onto the phone.
2. Open Game Bridge. The first time, it asks for two things in Android's settings:
   - **All files access**, so it can find game files in Downloads and your other folders.
   - **Install unknown apps**, so it can install the converted game. (Game Bridge restarts itself once after
     this.)
3. Your 32-bit games show up as cards. Tap **Convert**, wait, then tap **Install** on Android's screen.
4. Tap **Open** and play. Press and hold a card for more (Convert again, Remove, Delete file).

**Games with a game data file.** Some bigger games (Assassin's Creed Pirates, for example) come as an APK plus a
second, big file with their pictures, sounds and levels. Download sites call it the "cache", "OBB" or "data" file;
it ends in `.obb` (like `main.253.com.ubisoft.assassin.pirates.obb`) and often comes in a `.zip` with the APK. The
game won't start without it. Put the file, or the `.zip` it came in, in Downloads (or get the game as a bundle,
which includes it), and Game Bridge copies it into place when it installs the game. For games it knows (Pirates),
it also checks that it's the right, undamaged file. If a game needs one and Game Bridge can't find it, the card
says **Needs game data**; tap it for what to do.

## Games that have worked so far

> [!WARNING]
> **Most games have never been tried.** Only the games below have been tested, all on one phone (Pixel 10,
> Android 17). Any other game may not start, may crash partway through, may have missing sound or graphics, or
> may run much slower than it would on a phone with 32-bit support. Even the games below can behave differently
> on other phones or other versions of the game. Treat everything else as an experiment.

| Game | Version tested | How it runs |
|---|---|---|
| Card Wars | 1.12.9 | plays |
| Puzzle Craft | 1.1.3 | plays |
| Puzzle Craft 2 | 1.5.2 | plays |
| Assassin's Creed Pirates | 2.9.1 | plays (needs its game data file; Game Bridge adds a smoothness fix and a 60 fps cap) |
| Broken Age | 2.2.2 | plays |
| Angry Birds Classic | 8.0.3 | plays |

When a game uses phone functions the bridge doesn't know yet, the converter lists them; the game may then fail
when it reaches them.

## Good to know

- **No games are included.** Bring your own copies of games you own. This project is not connected to any game
  maker or store.
- **Converted games are signed by Game Bridge, not by their maker.** If the original game is still installed
  (for example from the Play Store), uninstall it first; that deletes its saved progress.
- **Old games get a small label change.** Android 17 refuses games made for Android 6 or older, so Game Bridge
  marks them as made for Android 7. Most games don't notice; a very old game could act differently.
- **Each phone has its own key.** Game Bridge makes a signing k

Nine numbered cards with prize values hidden behind them: 1, 10, 50, 100, 500, 1,000, 3,000, 5,000 and 10,000.

Open `index.html` in a browser. No build step or dependencies.

ShinjiK1/Social-Deduction-Game-NLP-Proje.readme:
# Catch The Larper

An online social deduction game used to collect hint data for training an imposter classifier.
Every player gets the same secret word except the **larper**, who only sees the category. Players
take turns giving short hints (25 characters max), then vote on who the larper is.

Play it at **https://catchthelarper.com**.

## How to play

1. Everyone gets the same secret word except one player, the **larper**, who only sees its category.
2. Players take turns giving a short hint (25 characters max) for a few rounds. Don't say the word itself.
3. Everyone votes for who they think the larper is.
4. If the larper alone gets the most votes, they're caught and each innocent scores +1. The larper then gets one guess at the word for +0.5.
5. Otherwise the larper scores +1. The larper wins ties.

## Rules and scoring (details)

- 3–12 players (3-6 recommended). The turn order is shuffled once per game and kept for every round. The number of rounds can be set from 1 to 5.
- The host picks which word categories are in play (all of them by default, at least one).
- An innocent's hint can't contain the secret word. The larper's hints are never rejected, because a rejection would tell them they had hit the word (although the innocents would then know who the larper is from this anyways).
- Voting: you can't vote for yourself, and votes can't be changed once locked in.
- The larper is **caught** only if they alone have the most votes. **The larper wins ties.**
  - Caught: each innocent gets +1, and the larper gets one guess at the word (+0.5 if correct).
  - Not caught: the larper gets +1.

## Running locally

```bash
npm install
npm run dev   # server on :3001, client on http://localhost:5173 (also reachable on your LAN)
```

Open several browser tabs to play as several players. Each tab is its own player.
If you refresh a page, you go back to the same seat.

## Supabase setup

1. Create a Supabase project and run `supabase/schema.sql` in its SQL editor.
2. Copy `server/.env.example` to `server/.env`, then set `SUPABASE_URL` and `SUPABASE_SECRET_KEY`
   (Project Settings → API keys → secret key). Only the server uses this key.

If Supabase isn't configured or an insert fails, finished games are appended to
`server/data/games.jsonl`, so no data is lost.

### Dev tables

When the server runs with `npm run dev`, the lobby shows a **Save to dev tables** toggle (on by
default, host-only). While it's on, that room's games go to `dev_games`, `dev_game_players` and
`dev_hints` (plus the `dev_game_transcripts` view) instead of the real dataset, or to
`server/data/games.dev.jsonl` as the fallback. Run `supabase/dev_schema.sql` once, after
`schema.sql`, to create them. `npm start` never shows the toggle and always logs to the real tables.

## Data collected

Nicknames are never stored. Each finished game is written to three tables:

| Table | Contents |
|---|---|
| `games` | `session_id` (one per room, shared by all of that room's games), word, category, settings, `larper_seat`, `vote_outcome` (`caught` / `tie` / `missed` / `no_votes`), the larper's guess |
| `game_players` | one row per seat: `is_larper`, `turn_position`, `vote_for_seat`, `score_delta`, `anon_id` |
| `hints` | `round`, `turn_index`, `seat`, `text`, `timed_out`, `ms_to_submit` (null if timed out). On a timeout, `text` is whatever was in the box, or `''` if it was empty (null before `rules_version` 2) |

`anon_id` stays the same for one player across all games in a room session. Use it to keep the
same people out of both the train and test sets. The `game_transcripts` view gives one row per
game with its hints in play order. If a rule change makes new games incomparable with older ones,
bump `RULES_VERSION` in `server/src/rooms.js`.

## Layout

```
server/src/index.js   Socket.IO event handlers and the static file server
server/src/rooms.js   room and game state machine, per-player views, building the logged record
server/src/text.js    hint and guess cleanup and word

paatsinsuwan/neuro-reflex-game.readme:
# Neuro Reflex

A browser reaction game based on the Stroop effect: press the color that matches either the word's ink color or the written word, before the timer runs out.

## Run

ES modules don't load from `file://`, so serve the folder:

```sh
python3 -m http.server 8000
```

Then open http://localhost:8000.

No build step. React, Radix Toggle Group and d3 are imported as ES modules from a CDN (see `js/vendor.js`).

## Structure

```
index.html            page shell
css/styles.css        compiled Tailwind styles (game)
css/site.css          site shell: header, intro, how-to-play, footer
js/main.js            entry point
js/vendor.js          third-party imports
js/constants.js       colors, trial timing, scoring
js/hooks/             useStroopGame (game logic), useContainerWidth
js/components/        UI components
```

## License

[MIT](LICENSE)

HeyItsDavis/catan-web.readme:
# Catan Web (moddable)

A browser-based, moddable take on Catan for playing online with friends.
Create a room, send the link, play. Everything — buildings, cards, decks,
resources, recipes — is data you can edit in the built-in mod editor.

* Play: https://heyitsdavis.github.io/catan-web/
* Architecture: [docs/ARCHITECTURE.md](docs/ARCHITECTURE.md)
* QA log (what is verified end to end, known issues): [docs/QA.md](docs/QA.md)

```
npm install
npm run dev      # local dev server
npm test         # engine tests
npm run build    # production build (deployed by GitHub Actions on push to main)
npm run e2e      # Playwright: two browsers play over PeerJS (needs internet; see docs/QA.md)
npm run e2e:pages  # same, against the production build served under /catan-web/

cyber-arena-ai/octagon.readme: **Octagon** is the game engine behind [CyberArena](https://cyber-arena.ai), a benchmark in which two AI agents play **attack-and-defense CTF** against each other in an isolated network sandbox. Each agent attacks the opponent's copy of a vulnerable service for a flag that rotates every round, while patching its own copy; the arena verifies every capture and health check. This repository spins up the Docker networks and per-team containers, plants and rotates flags, probes service health, runs the round loop, and drives LLM coding agents for both sides through an MCP channel. Harnesses are mixable per team: Claude Code, Codex, opencode, Gemini CLI, Grok CLI, Kimi, Qwen Code, the DeepSeek harness, OpenHands and NexAU, plus `script` and `idle` placeholders for solo and verification runs. - **Paper:** [arXiv:2610.19005](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.19005) · [alphaXiv](https://www.alphaxiv.org/abs/2610.19005) - **Leaderboard and match replays:** [cyber-arena.ai](https://cyber-arena.ai) - **Challenges:** [cyber-arena-ai/challenge-warehouse](https://github.com/cyber-arena-ai/challenge-warehouse) (bundled here as a git submodule) System design: [docs/UML/overview.md](docs/UML/overview.md). Writing a new challenge: [docs/CHALLENGE_AUTHORING_SOP.md](docs/CHALLENGE_AUTHORING_SOP.md). ## Repository layout Flat package layout — every directory below is importable by its own name (`from gamemgr import …`). The top level splits into core code, support assets, and generated dirs (`runs/`, git-ignored). ``` main.py CLI entry: setup / start / teardown │ ├─ gamemgr/ GameMgr, round loop, Timeline, events, FastAPI + MCP surface, config loader ├─ orchestrator/ Docker container + network lifecycle (infra/ + per-team compose) ├─ flag/ FlagServer + FlagStore — plant / rotate / submit ├─ health/ HealthChecker + HealthPoller — functionality probes ├─ facility/ Facility boundary: status/events/exec ports + SSH/in-process adapters ├─ mcpgateway/ On-net MCP gateway container — agents' tool surface, forwards to GameMgr REST ├─ agents/ Agent managers + transports, one adapter per harness (claude · codex · opencode · …) ├─ challenges/ Challenge contract (interface ABC) + auto-discovery registry ├─ challenge-warehouse/ Challenge implementations — git submodule, grouped by contributor ├─ apirouter/ Egress gateway + LLM metering proxy (self-contained service) ├─ models/ Shared data models (topology, agent config) │ ├─ config/ Game YAML configs + team-image Dockerfiles (docker/) ├─ dockerfiles/ v3 infra/base image build contexts (agent/base + agent/ · mcp-gateway · flag-service · health-poller · api-router-cfg) ├─ panel/ panel.html live dashboard (served at /panel) ├─ vis/ Realtime topology visualizer — standalone read-only HTML graph ├─ scripts/ Helper scripts (build_images.sh, update_challenges.sh, …) ├─ tests/ Test suite (~1,200 tests; run scoped to tests/ — see below) ├─ docs/ Design docs + UML (docs/UML/) │ └─ runs/ Generated run artifacts: events.jsonl, panel snapshots · git-ignored ``` Challenge packages live in the `challenge-warehouse` submodule but are stitched into the `challenges` namespace via `__path__`, so each still imports as `challenges.`. # Ashen Crown · 灰烬王冠

A fantasy card duel game for phones and browsers. Pick one of six classes, fight through an eight-foe Adventure, or build a 25-card deck and face a random AI in Quick Match, or play a friend online with a room code. Plays in English, Chinese and Japanese.

Live: https://ashen-crown.hermes-eris.com

## Layout
- `src/game.html` — the whole game (HTML, CSS and JavaScript in one file). Edit this.
- `src/build.py` — wraps the game into the site: writes `index.html` and `sw.js` in the repo root.
- `src/sw.template.js` — offline service worker template (cache name is stamped per build).
- `peerjs.min.js` — PeerJS 1.5.4 client for Play a Friend (peer-to-peer; signalling via the free PeerJS cloud server). Add `?peer=host:port` to the URL to use a self-hosted PeerServer instead.
- `ios/` — iOS app (Xcode project wrapping the game for TestFlight / App Store). See `ios/README.md`.
- `privacy.html` — privacy policy (linked from App Store Connect).
- Root: the published site (GitHub Pages serves `main` / root), icons, `manifest.webmanifest`, `CNAME`.

## Update the site
```
python3 src/build.py      # also syncs ios/AshenCrown/Web
git commit -am "Update game" && git push
```

keanfreeman/shogun2-veteran-upgrades-pat.readme:
# Veteran Upgrades: Patched Edition

*A single-player mod for **Total War: Shogun 2***

Works in all three campaigns: **Sengoku Jidai**, **Rise of the Samurai** and **Fall of the Samurai**.
Playing the **Master of Strategy Sengoku (MoSS)** overhaul? Use the [MoSS version](#two-editions).

[![Verify patchers](https://github.com/keanfreeman/shogun2-veteran-upgrades-patched/actions/workflows/verify.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/keanfreeman/shogun2-veteran-upgrades-patched/actions/workflows/verify.yml)

Your clan earns a point for every battle it fights and spends points on **upgrades for each unit type**:

- **Stats:** melee attack and defence, armour, morale, accuracy, charge, speed, reload, ammunition,
  range, bonus vs cavalry
- **Traits:** fire while hidden, camouflage, guerrilla deployment, fatigue resistance, Scare Enemies
- **Abilities** such as War Cry, Rally, Inspire, Rapid Volley, Fire by Rank, Pike Wall or Wedge

Upgrades apply at once to every unit of that type, including the ones already in your armies. AI clans
play too. Most of this needs a **small, reversible patch** to one game file (included); without it only
the basic stats, Scare Enemies and fatigue resistance work.

| Pick a unit type... | ...and buy its upgrades |
|---|---|
| ![The Veterans list: every unit type you can recruit, by category](docs/images/unit-list-sengoku.png) | ![Yari Ashigaru's upgrades: stats, traits and abilities](docs/images/yari-ashigaru-upgrades.png) |

## Two editions

| Edition | For | Download |
|---|---|---|
| **Patched Edition** | The base game: Sengoku, Rise of the Samurai, Fall of the Samurai | [Latest release](https://github.com/keanfreeman/shogun2-veteran-upgrades-patched/releases/latest) |
| **Patched Edition for MoSS** *(new, pre-release)* | The [Master of Strategy Sengoku](mod-moss/README.md) overhaul: its units, clans and ability names | [moss-v1.0.0](https://github.com/keanfreeman/shogun2-veteran-upgrades-patched/releases/tag/moss-v1.0.0) |

Both use the same patch. **Enable only one Veteran Upgrades mod at a time**, including the Workshop's
[Veteran Upgrades](https://github.com/keanfreeman/shogun2-veteran-upgrades), which needs no patch:
they all change the same game file.

## Before you start

- **Steam version on Windows** (or Linux through Proton). The native Mac/Linux versions aren't supported.
- **Single-player only.** Online play uses Valve Anti-Cheat, and a changed game file could get your
  account banned. The mod switches multiplayer and drop-in battles off; **restore the game before
  playing online** (see below).
- After a Steam update the patcher may refuse to run until the mod is updated. That's on purpose.

## Installing

1. Download the zip from the release (see the table above). On Windows, right-click it → **Properties**
   → tick **Unblock**, then extract it.
2. Quit Shogun 2. Copy the `.pack` and `.png` into the game's `data` folder (Steam: right-click
   Shogun 2 → **Manage** → **Browse local files** → `data`).
3. Run **`patcher/Install patch.bat`** (Linux: `python3 patcher/patch_game.py install`). It should end
   with *"Patched (patch version 4)"*. If Windows warns, click **More info** → **Run anyway**.
4. Tick the mod in the launcher (MoSS edition: also MoSS's packs) and start a new campaign.

On the campaign map, click **Veterans** (below the advisor button), pick a unit type, choose upgrades and
press **OK**. **Reset** refunds a unit type for a small fee. Some abilities also need their usual research
or a general's skill; the tooltip says which.

**Updating from 1.0:** replace the files in `data` and run `Install patch.bat` again (2.0 needs patch v4).

## Uninstalling / before playing multiplayer

Quit the game and run **`patcher/Restore game.bat`** (Linux: `python3 patcher/patch_game.py restore`),
or use Steam's **Verify integrity of game files**. Then untick the mod. Restoring doesn't switch the
game's "allow drop-in battles" setting back on; tick it again if you want it.

# Ogrimwar

Guide de progression Dofus 3.7 pour faire tous les succès en team, étape par étape dans l'ordre du **GP0 de Ganymède** : pour chaque étape, les succès qu'elle termine ou fait avancer, les rappels « ×4 », les fiches de donjon et la page Dofus pour les Noobs en panneau. Profils multiples (un par team), progression gardée dans le navigateur, transférable par code.

Site : https://0214649.github.io/ogrimwar/

## Sources

- **Guides Ganymède** (https://ganymede-app.com) : chargés en direct depuis leur API publique par le navigateur. Aucun contenu Ganymède n'est stocké dans ce dépôt. `route.json` ne contient que des numéros d'étapes (quelle plage de quel guide suit chaque étape du GP0).
- **Noms et descriptions officiels des succès (FR)** : lus en local dans les fichiers du jeu installé (copie, lecture seule) par `tools/extract_game.py` ; rien du client n'est stocké ici à part ces textes dans `ach.json`.
- **Succès et objectifs** : [DofusWiki](https://dofuswiki.fandom.com) (Fandom), sous licence [CC-BY-SA 3.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/). `ach.json` est dérivé de leurs modules `Datatable/Achievements`, `Datatable/*/ILLs` et des pages de donjons, et il est distribué sous la même licence.

Site non officiel. Dofus © Ankama Games.

## Reconstruire les données

```sh
python3 tools/fetch_guides.py tools/cache   # guides Ganymède (lent exprès : leur API limite les rafales)
python3 tools/expand.py tools/cache         # plages de sous-guides citées par chaque étape du GP0
python3 tools/make_route.py                 # -> route.json
python3 tools/build_ach.py                  # -> ach.json (wiki dans tools/wiki/)
```

`tools/fetch_guides.py` attend `tools/cache/gp_list.json` (`https://ganymede-app.com/api/guides?status=gp`).

## Vérifier les données

```sh
python3 tools/audit.py   # pages exemple/bonus, catégories et noms du jeu, doublons, donjons, couverture
```

dethialaw/pocket-imperium.desc: Pocket Imperium space-conquest strategy game in Java — OOP design patterns, AI opponents, Swing GUI, save/load
dethialaw/pocket-imperium.readme:
# Pocket Imperium — Java OOP board game

A Java implementation of **Pocket Imperium**, a space-conquest strategy board game for 3 players. Each player commands a fleet of ships on a board of hexagonal systems grouped into sectors. Over 9 rounds, players expand, explore and exterminate to control the most valuable sectors.

The focus of the project is a clean object model built on classic design patterns, with a Swing interface, AI opponents and save/load support.

![Java](https://img.shields.io/badge/Java-17+-ED8B00?logo=openjdk&logoColor=white)
![Swing](https://img.shields.io/badge/GUI-Swing-5382A1)

---

## Features

- **1 to 3 human players**. Empty seats are filled by **virtual players** (bots) with an **offensive** or a **defensive** strategy.
- **Full game loop over 9 rounds**:
  1. **Command phase**: each player secretly orders the three commands *Expand*, *Explore* and *Exterminate*. The more players pick the same command in the same turn, the fewer actions each one gets (3 / 2 / 1).
  2. **Sustain phase**: systems that hold more ships than they can support lose the extra ships.
  3. **Scoring phase**: each player scores one sector they occupy, and the player controlling **Tri-Prime** (the central sector) scores a bonus sector.
  4. **Final scoring**: system values are doubled. The game also ends early if a player has no ships left.
- **Swing graphical interface**: board view refreshed after every action, game menu (*Nouvelle Partie / Sauvegarder / Charger / Quitter*), rules and about dialogs. Players enter their actions in the console.
- **Save and load** a game in progress using Java serialisation, through a file chooser.
- **Javadoc** comments on all classes and public methods.

---

## Object-oriented design

| Concept | Where |
|---|---|
| **Singleton** | `Jeu` is the single game instance (`Jeu.getInstance()`), and is restored after loading a save |
| **Strategy** | `StrategieJeu` interface with `StrategieOffensive` and `StrategieDefensive`, injected into `JoueurVirtuel` |
| **Command** (abstract class + polymorphism) | abstract `Command` with `Expand`, `Explore` and `Exterminate`, each implementing `handleCommand(maxActions)` |
| **Inheritance** | `JoueurVirtuel extends Joueur` |
| **Observer-like refresh** | the game notifies the GUI (`notifierMiseAJour()`) after each action so the board is redrawn |
| **Serialisation** | every model class implements `Serializable`. Custom `writeObject` / `readObject` methods exclude the GUI and re-bind the singleton |
| **Enums** | `Couleur` (player colours), `TypeCommand` (EXPAND / EXPLORE / EXTERMINATE) |

### Main classes

```
Jeu ─────────────── game state & round loop (Singleton)
 ├── Joueur ◄─────── JoueurVirtuel ──► StrategieJeu ◄── StrategieOffensive / StrategieDefensive
 │     ├── Ships           (a player's fleet)
 │     └── Command ◄────── Expand / Explore / Exterminate
 ├── Plateau ────── board setup (sectors, systems, initial placement)
 │     └── Sector ── Hexagone ── Position / Localisation
 └── JeuGUI ─────── Swing interface (board view, menus, save/load)
```

---

## Getting started

### Requirements

- JDK **17 or newer**

### Compile and run

```bash
# from the project root
javac -encoding UTF-8 -d bin src/pocketimperium/*.java
java -cp bin pocketimperium.Jeu
```

The Swing window opens. Start a game from the menu (**Nouvelle Partie**), then follow the prompts in the terminal (number of human players, command order, moves…).

You can also open the folder in **VS Code** (Java extension pack) or **IntelliJ IDEA** and run `pocketimperium.Jeu`.

### Documentation

To generate the Javadoc and open `docs/index.html` in a browser:

```bash
javadoc -encoding UTF-8 -d docs -sourcepath src pocketimperium
```

---

## Project structure

```
.
├── src/pocketimperium/   # Java sources (model, game logic, strategies, GUI)
└── .vscode/           # VS Code Java project settings
```

---

## What I learned

- Modelling a non-trivial board-game rule set as a set of collaborati

dudwns0921/gamedev-kit-board.readme:
# gamedev-kit-board

The dashboard of [claude-gamedev-kit](https://github.com/dudwns0921/claude-gamedev-kit): every game on your machine on one page — what waits on you across games, then each game's stages, review and assets — redrawn as the games change.

It runs on your own machine, next to the games. The kit installs and starts it; you do not clone this repository by hand.

## Start it

In any game that uses the kit, ask Claude to start the dashboard (or run it yourself):

```bash
python3 <kit>/skills/board/scripts/board.py serve
```

That clones this repository to `~/.config/gamedev-kit/board-app`, builds it (once per version), starts it on `http://localhost:3100`, and sends the game's board. Needs git and Node.js.
There is no sign-in: it is yours, on your machine. Run `serve` once in each game that should appear; after that every Claude turn in that game sends its board.

`serve --status` · `serve --stop`. After a restart of the machine, `serve` starts it again.

## From your phone or another computer

The server listens on your machine only. Reach it through one of:

- **Tailscale** (phone and laptop): install it on both devices, then on the machine running the dashboard `tailscale serve --bg 3100`. Open the https address it prints — only your own devices reach it.
- **SSH**: `ssh -L 3100:127.0.0.1:3100 <your machine>`, then open `http://127.0.0.1:3100` on the device you are on.

Do not open the port to the internet, and do not use `tailscale funnel` — there is no password; who can reach it can use it.
The app answers only to `localhost`, `127.0.0.1` and a Tailscale name (`*.ts.net`; more in `BOARD_HOSTS`, comma-separated), and takes a change only from its own pages — another site open in your browser cannot reach it.

## What it does not do

It does not chat and does not run anything in a game — it only signals. Pick the answers on the Review tab (an option, approve, OK, "not needed") and send them:
they go to the game's inbox, the game's open Claude session is woken for them — or the next session you open picks them up — and the session does the work.
The page follows as the session redraws the board.

## Run it by hand (development)

```bash
npm install
INGEST_TOKEN=dev npm run dev
```

Data goes to `.data/`. Point a game at it with `GAMEDEV_BOARD_URL=http://localhost:3000` and `GAMEDEV_BOARD_TOKEN=dev` (in the environment or `~/.config/gamedev-kit/board.env`), then `board.py push`.

It has no sign-in, so it is not for hosting where others can reach it.

## How it fits together

| Path | What |
|---|---|
| `POST /api/ingest/<game>/check` | the kit lists the pictures and sounds its board points to (named by content); the answer is the ones missing |
| `PUT /api/ingest/<game>/file/<name>` | one picture or sound |
| `PUT /api/ingest/<game>/summary` | the board as data (`board.json`) — everything the dashboard draws |
| `DELETE /api/ingest/<game>` | takes a game off (the next push from it puts it back) |
| `/` | your games |
| `/g/<game>` | one game: overview · review · stages · assets; told over `/g/<game>/events` the moment a newer board arrives or its inbox changes (↻ reads again and reconnects) |
| `/g/<game>/inbox` · `/g/<game>/act` | where sent answers stand · send answers to the game's inbox (the only thing it writes into a game) |

Storage keys, in `.data/`: `games/<game>/summary.json` · `f/<hash>.<ext>`.

leokayehsu-bit/grimoire.readme:
# Grimoire

A co-op "one sees, the others read" party game. The **Medium** sits at a séance table covered in cursed relics but can't read the book. The **Scholars** hold the grimoire but never see the table. Talk it through and cleanse every relic before the spirit's wrath boils over.

## Play

- Open `index.html` through any static server (or the `grimoire` preview, port 8778).
- **Create a room** → share the 4-letter code or the invite link → one player picks Medium, the rest pick Scholar → host presses **Begin**.
- Rooms use [PeerJS](https://peerjs.com): the free PeerJS cloud server only introduces players, then game data goes browser-to-browser. Voice isn't carried, so play in one room or on a call.
- Add `?local` to the URL for offline testing with several tabs in one browser (BroadcastChannel, no internet).

**One screen:** “Play on one screen” on the main menu skips rooms entirely. This computer is the Medium, and the Scholars read a **printed grimoire**. The print card prints the book for the chosen edition (pages you've unlocked, or every page), in the smudged version when Damned is picked; a level that adds a page offers to print just that page. The printable book is a plain link: `?print&edition=N&upto=L` (or `&all`, or `&only=<relic>`, plus `&smudged`; `&noauto` skips the print dialog). “Read the grimoire” has a print button too.

**Ratings:** every win earns 1–3 candles (cleansed; no offenses; under 60% of the time limit). Each browser keeps its best candles and time per level and difficulty (in `grimoire.progress.v1`), shown on the end screen, the level card, the level list (with chapter totals) and the main menu.

**App + offline:** the site is an installable web app (`manifest.webmanifest`, `sw.js`, icons from `tools/icons.sh`). The service worker fetches the page network-first (so online players always run the latest release) and serves the `?v=`-stamped scripts from its cache, so one-screen play, the grimoire and printing work offline. It is skipped on localhost unless you add `?sw`. `tools/publish.sh` stamps `sw.js` so installed apps update.

**Sound:** everything is synthesised in `js/audio.js` (no audio files). Effects and music run through separate buses into a shared stone-room reverb. The séance score is adaptive: `setIntensity({ wrath, strikes, remaining })` drives a drone, organ chords and a music box when calm, then a quickening heartbeat, trembling strings, a choir and a ticking clock as the wrath rises, with booms in the final 15 seconds and stingers at 50/75/90% wrath. Scholars hear the score and every offense or cleansing through the Medium's status updates. Menus get a quiet music-box version. Music and effects volumes (bottom-left 🔊) are saved per browser.

**Colour labels:** Settings (bottom-left ⚙) → Colour labels names every colour a relic uses — candles, bell ribbon, crystal-ball mist, lantern flame, pendulum crystal, apothecary liquids, gramophone record, the light under the door and the rings in Palm Reading — for colourblind players. Each relic renders a hidden `.cb-label`; `body.cb` shows them.

**The Medium's table:** relics sit on a wood-grain séance table (`.seance-table`) under flickering candlelight with drifting dust (a small canvas), each on a velvet cloth with brass corners and an engraved nameplate; a red wax seal is pressed on when a relic is cleansed. Every relic has its own sounds (pinched candles, burning cards, dial clicks and a latch, glass chimes and cracks, chisel on stone, bone clatter, pouring salt, bubbling jars, a crackly gramophone tune, wings…) on top of the shared offense/cleansing cues; quiet ones are scaled by `BOOST` in `js/audio.js`.

**What Scholars see:** only the offense marks (the Music Box page depends on them). No timer, wrath meter, cleansed count or relic names, so the Medium has to describe the table. They still feel the wrath: the red vignette closes in and throbs faster, the screen shakes on offenses, glows on cleansings, and the music follows the

SolbiatiAlessandro/parley-post-train.readme:
# parley-post-train

Post-training small open models on [Parley](https://github.com/Metta-AI/cogame-parley), a five-player
talk-and-shoot party game from Softmax's Coworld platform. Built on the night of 2026-10-14 → 15 by
Tashi (Alessandro Solbiati's agent) on a Mac mini, with the model served and trained on Modal GPUs.

**Start with the reports:**

- [`reports/night-report-2026-10-15.md`](reports/night-report-2026-10-15.md) — what ran, the numbers,
  nine failure modes with fixes, cost, next steps; appendices list every game and every training step.
- [`reports/rl-literature-review.md`](reports/rl-literature-review.md) — the review (60 sources) behind
  the RL algorithm choice, with a concrete spec.
- [`reports/thinking-patterns-game3.md`](reports/thinking-patterns-game3.md) — what Qwen3.5-4B does in
  its thinking during a game, from 19 full traces.

## Result in one paragraph

Qwen3.5-4B plays complete, legal games of Parley out of the box once the decoder is limited to legal
names. Its thinking mode is long (median ~6,000 tokens per call) and ignores prompt-level length requests.
Three iterations of self-play RL (LoRA, leave-one-out advantage over the five seats of a game, token-level
loss, 4 clipped steps per iteration) produced no measurable change: in 17 evaluation games one trained seat
against four untouched seats scored 0.441 ± 0.091 (mean placement, standard error) versus 0.515 for the
untouched seats. The policy barely moved; the budget ($40 of GPU) bought a working loop and a catalogue of
what breaks, not a trained player.

## How it fits together

```
Parley game (Docker, Mac)  --Anthropic Messages request-->  recorder.py (Mac)
recorder.py  --OpenAI chat request-->  vLLM serving Qwen (+ LoRA adapters) on a Modal GPU (modal_qwen.py)
recorder.py  --reply-->  game; every request/reply saved to runs/<game>/calls.jsonl
hub.py       --landing page-->  paused step-through replays of every recorded game
rl_iterate.py:  rl_rollouts.py (N games at once) -> build_trajectories.py -> modal_train.py (LoRA update) -> redeploy
```

| File | What it does |
|---|---|
| `modal_qwen.py` | Serves the model with vLLM on one Modal GPU. Starts on the first request, stops after 10 idle minutes. Serves LoRA adapters listed in `/adapters/active.json` on the `parley-adapters` volume. `PARLEY_APP=name modal deploy modal_qwen.py` deploys a second server. |
| `recorder.py` | Sits between the game and the GPU. Translates the game's request, builds a JSON schema per call so only legal names can be produced, streams the thinking to the live page, applies Qwen's thinking-budget cutoff, retries across server restarts, saves everything. `--route slot=adapter` serves one seat from another adapter (mixed tables). |
| `run_game.py` | Plays one game: wakes the GPU, starts the Parley container, connects five players with the operator prompt, waits for the scores, then starts a replay server for the finished game. |
| `viewer.html`, `replay.html`, `replay_frame.html` | Live page and paused step-through replay: Parley's own table view next to each model call's prompt, secret cards, thinking and answer. |
| `hub.py`, `index.html` | Landing page over `runs/`: every game, its state, and its replay. |
| `rl_rollouts.py` | Runs N games in parallel, each with its own recorder and ports; evaluation mode puts a trained adapter in one rotating seat. |
| `build_trajectories.py` | Turns finished games into training rows: per-seat reward (placement score minus an optional thinking-length penalty), leave-one-out advantage, every call of the seat, injected text masked. |
| `modal_train.py` | Modal functions: `make_adapter` (identity LoRA) and `train_step` (clipped policy-gradient update on a LoRA, token-level loss, optional KL, KL-to-base logging). |
| `rl_iterate.py` | One RL iteration end to end, or `--evaluate K` for the mixed-table evaluation. |

## Settings used

Qwen3.5-4B (`Qwen/Qwen3.5-4B`), vLLM 0.31.0, one H100 (L40S for the first game). Parley pinned at comm

DeprivedPeasant/ape-escape-decomp-port.desc: Readable decompilation and native port of Ape Escape (PS1, SCUS-94423): hand-ported C verified against the original instructions. No game data included.
DeprivedPeasant/ape-escape-decomp-port.readme:
# Ape Escape decomp → native port

A readable decompilation of **Ape Escape** (USA, SCUS-94423), leading to a native port in the spirit of the Super
Mario 64 and Zelda projects. Original game functions are hand-ported to structured, named C and **verified one by one
against the original MIPS instructions**. The port then runs on native systems (renderer, audio, input, file I/O):
there is no emulator, no recompiler and no machine-translated code.

> **No game data is included.** This repository contains only original code, tools and documentation. You need
> your own legally obtained copy of the game. Disc images, extracted files, BIOS files, decompiler output and game
> text are never committed (see `.gitignore`).

## Status

- About 1,500 original functions are ported and differentially verified. The ledger is `tools/verified.csv`;
  `uv run python tools/check_verified.py` checks it.
- The **game host** (`src/game/`) runs `main`'s mode dispatch (boot -> title, matching the original) and the ported
  `Mode_Stage` loop on one RAM image:
  - area load, the player (`PlayerUpdate`), monkeys and their AI, enemies, collision, camera, HUD, pause menu and
    stage fades;
  - the Monkey Net catch;
  - every frame of areas 01, 02, 05 and 44 matches the original instructions byte for byte.
- The **native viewer** (`src/app/`, SDL3 + OpenGL) runs the real game logic and renders terrain, props and sky.
  It reaches no missing functions in areas 01 and 02. Drawing of characters, HUD and effects from game data is still
  in progress.
- **Overlays:** nearly all mode overlays (boot, intro, title, save menu, Stage Clear, Special Area Enter, minigames)
  and the area overlays 18C, 1A0 and 1A8 are ported. Most area and boss overlays are not yet.
- The project is paused until about 2026-10-23; `notes/port/paused_2026-10-15.md` lists the open work.

See [notes/HANDOFF.md](notes/HANDOFF.md) for the full picture and [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md) for the project rules.

## Layout

| Path | Contents |
|---|---|
| `src/` | Portable C by subsystem: ported game code (`ae_*.c`), the game host (`src/game/`), native systems and viewer. See [src/README.md](src/README.md). |
| `tools/mips/` | MIPS interpreter (test oracle only) and the differential checkers `check_*.py`. |
| `tools/verified.csv`, `tools/mips/check_exclusions.csv` | Verification ledger and the registry of declared, evidence-backed comparison exclusions. |
| `tools/` | Extraction, dump, export and inventory scripts; Ghidra scripts. |
| `notes/` | Findings: formats, structures, function maps, per-module port notes (`notes/port/`). |
| `disc/`, `extract/`, `bios/` | Your local copies (gitignored, never committed). |

## Getting started

1. Install [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) and a MinGW-w64 GCC. On Windows, GCC 8+ on `PATH` is enough for the
   checkers.
2. Put your own Redump `SCUS-94423` bin/cue in `disc/`. Keep it as bin/cue: converting to ISO loses the XA streams.
3. Extract it:
   - extract the disc filesystem to `extract/disc/` with `dumpsxiso -l`;
   - unpack the archive members with `uv run python tools/unpack_kkiiddzz.py`, which produces `extract/members/`.

   See [notes/00-setup.md](notes/00-setup.md) and [notes/01-disc-layout.md](notes/01-disc-layout.md).
4. Run a checker, for example `uv run python tools/mips/check_game_area.py` (the integrated game host against the
   original). For the native viewer, see `tools/codex/build_native_viewer.py --help` (it expects the SDL3
   MinGW development package under `extract/codex/deps/`).

Optional analysis tools (not included; versions in `notes/00-setup.md`): Ghidra 12.1.2 with `ghidra_psx_ldr`,
PCSX-Redux, splat / spimdisasm (`uv run splat ...`).

## Contributing

- **Port one function per original function** as readable, structured C: named locals, named field offsets and
  globals (`#define`), and no simulated registers, delay slots or per-PC labels.
- **Add a differential checker,** or extend one in `tools/mips/`, that runs the original ins

- Live: https://lesanf.github.io/hero-lord-web/ (GitHub Pages, rebuilt from `main` by Actions; only the latest deployment is ever served)

## 원작 그래픽 / 리마스터 그래픽

The game ships both art sets. The page starts straight into the game with the
last choice (first visit: 원작) and keeps a small **원작 그래픽 | 리마스터** switch

## How it works

The APK contains no native game code. `libgodot_android.so` is the stock Godot
4.6 runtime; the game is compiled GDScript (`.gdc`) plus assets stored loose
under `assets/`, already imported for the GL Compatibility renderer. So the port
is a repack, not a rewrite:

```
APK ─unzip─▶ exported Godot project ─pack─▶ hero-lord.pck ─split─▶ 64 MB parts
                     +  web/override.cfg + web/web_shim.gd (web-only autoload)
official Godot 4.6 web template (godot.wasm, nothreads) + web/index.html ─▶ static site
```

| step | file | notes |
|---|---|---|
| inventory | `tools/inventory.py` | what is in the APK, no extraction |
| extract | `tools/extract_project.py` | `assets/` → `build/project/`, drops Android-only files |
| shrink | `tools/minify_json.py`, `tools/compress_audio.sh` | JSON whitespace (19 → 10 MB) and PCM → QOA audio inside the same `AudioStreamWAV` resources (80 → 16 MB, done by the Godot 4.6 binary itself, headless) |
| pack | `tools/pack_pck.py` | PCK v2 writer, stdlib only, `tools/test_pack_pck.py` round-trips it |
| assemble | `tools/build_web.py` | pulls the 9.5 MB web template out of the 1.25 GB official tpz with HTTP range requests (sha256 pinned), splits the PCK, writes `index.html` |
| all of it | `./build.sh game.apk` | ~25 s on a laptop; the site is 157 MB of game data + 38 MB of engine |

`web/index.html` shows a loading screen (pixel-art backdrop in `web/img/loading.jpg`,
progress bar with MB and %) while it downloads the parts, hands the buffer to the engine with
`preloadFile` and starts it with `--main-pack … -- art=<remembered choice>`. The
page-level art switch talks to the game through `window.heroLordSetArt`
(exposed by the shim with `JavaScriptBridge`) and listens for `herolord-art`
events the shim fires when the game changes it. Single-threaded template, so
no COOP/COEP headers are needed and any static host works.

## Web-only shim

Nothing in the game is modified. `web/override.cfg` is packed next to
`project.binary` and registers one autoload, `web/web_shim.gd`, which:

- turns on `emulate_touch_from_mouse` (the in-game menus only listen to touch) and keeps the real left click away from the GUI, so every click reaches the game exactly once, through the same router A

Bencepapa/chipgrove.desc: Abstract factory game in a circuit board
Bencepapa/chipgrove.readme:
# Chipgrove

A retro-computer factory puzzle game. Mine bits, notes, pixels and colours from pixel-art fields, fit tetromino-shaped factories together, and feed old machines: bytes for the 6510 CPU, SID tunes for the jukebox, sprites and chars for the VIC-II.

Everything is wired either by making ports touch or by laying a few precious tubes, and every factory plays its part in a generated chiptune.

## What's here

| Path | What it is |
|---|---|
| `prototype/index.html` | The playable prototype, a single self-contained HTML file. Open it in a browser. |
| `data/chipgrove-data.xlsx` | Balancing workbook: materials, parts, recipes with per-item margins, order types and economy constants, copied from the prototype. |
| `docs/design.md` | Current rules and the roadmap. |

## The prototype

Two modes:

- **Puzzles**: small 8×8 boards with a fixed set of parts. A level is solved when every input on every user has received an item. Score rewards working parts, unused tubes (max 3) and unused relay poles, plus a bonus for a layout that differs from the designer's. Includes a level editor with custom part shapes and ports, a solution builder and shareable level codes.
- **Big map**: a 32×32 scrollable map. Buy parts from the drawer by dragging them out, fill orders that pay per item, and expand towards rarer fields.

Progress and edited levels are stored in the browser's `localStorage`.

## Status

The prototype was built in a few long iterative sessions as a single file. The next step is to split it into modules (data, simulation, audio, rendering, editor) and load the game data from one source instead of the hard-coded tables, so the workbook can drive balancing.

milothorhager/kid-game-studio.readme:
# 🎮 Kid Game Studio

**Your own video game team.** Kids (about 9-13) say what game they want, and Claude designs it, builds it, tests it,
and puts it on the Mac's Dock as a real game. Up to 4 players, keyboard + game controllers, original music and
art. Along the way kids learn how real studios work: break big ideas into small steps, build a quick version,
playtest, keep the good ideas, toss the rest.

No coding. No menus. Kids just talk (or voice-type) to Claude.

> "I want a game where my cousins defend our treehouse from a construction crew, exactly like PixelJunk Monsters."
> → a 4-player tower-defense game with 40 levels, a world map, bosses and rock music, built over a few afternoons.

---

## ⚡ Set it up (a grown-up, about 10 minutes, once)

You need a **Mac** and the **Claude app** with a plan that includes Claude Code ([claude.ai/download](https://claude.ai/download)).

1. Open the Claude app and click **Code**. Pick any folder (your home folder is fine).
2. Paste this into the chat:

   ```
   Please install the Kid Game Studio plugin by running this in the terminal:
   curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/milothorhager/kid-game-studio/main/install.sh | bash
   ```

   (Already use Claude Code in a terminal? You can instead run
   `/plugin install kid-game-studio --marketplace milothorhager/kid-game-studio`.)

3. Start a **new** Code session, choose the new **Games** folder in your home folder, and paste:

   ```
   Set up my game studio.
   ```

   Claude checks the Mac, asks before downloading anything (the free **Godot** game engine and a few small tools,
   no admin password needed), makes the Games folder, and asks you a few questions about your kid.

4. Hand it to your kid. They can say anything, like *"I want to make a game where dragons race on the moon"*.

**Best settings:** in the menu next to the chat box, pick the **Opus** model and effort **High** for building.
Big builds use a lot of your plan's usage; the studio builds small playable steps first so nothing is wasted.

## 🕹️ Play a friend's game

Your friend invites you (their Claude does it). Then just open Claude in your Games folder: it tells you about the
invitation and puts the game on your Dock. Or paste:

```
Please get the game <friend's-github-name>/<game-name> from GitHub and put it on my Dock so I can play it.
```

## 🤝 Make games together

Games are saved privately on GitHub and shared only with invited friends. Kids never see GitHub; they just say:

| The kid says | What happens |
|---|---|
| "Share my game with Sam" | Claude uploads it privately and invites Sam |
| "Get Sam's game" | It downloads it and adds a Dock button |
| "I made Sam's boss scarier, send it to Sam" | It sends a **suggestion** to Sam's game |
| (Sam opens Claude) | "Your friend has an idea for your game: a scarier boss! Want to try it?" Sam tries it, then **keeps it** or **tosses it** |

That's how real software teams work (pull requests and code review), without any of the complicated parts.
GitHub needs an account for each kid; GitHub requires users to be 13+, so younger kids use an account a grown-up
manages. A grown-up does a one-time sign-in during setup.

## 🧠 What's inside

The studio is a set of **skills**. Claude loads only the ones a game needs:

- **Studio:** `game-studio` (the main loop: talk like a kid's game team, scope, build, test, ship, teach),
  `new-game`, `share-games`, `studio-setup`, `improve-studio`
- **Craft:** `pixel-art`, `low-poly-3d`, `game-music`, `sound-effects`, `icon-and-splash`
- **Game parts:** `player-join`, `little-sibling-mode`, `platformer`, `platform-fighter`, `beat-em-up`,
  `enemy-waves`, `boss-battles`, `warned-hazards`, `weather-and-night`, `level-machine`, `buddies-and-rides`,
  `weapons-and-pickups`, `story-movies`, `character-maker`, `photo-booth`, `tower-defense`, `farm-defense`,
  `survivors-arena`, `world-map-and-saves`, `online-multiplayer`
- **Helpers** (cheaper models for big builds): `art-maker`, `sound-maker`

PrinceKay145/skytec-metacritic.readme:
# Metacritic games crawler **Live demo: **. The crawler monitor is at [/monitor](https://p01--metacritic--l6tcpp2w27x4.code.run/monitor). It runs on Northflank's free tier (London) with a managed PostgreSQL. Summaries and embeddings come from OpenRouter, and the crawl runs hourly inside the app. On the public site **Run now** needs the admin token. To run everything on your own machine, follow the [demo walkthrough](#demo-walkthrough) (Docker) or [local development](#local-development). Every hour this service picks 20 games from Metacritic that it hasn't processed yet that day, then adds them to its database or updates them. For each game it stores the cover, platforms with Metascore and user score, developer, description and video link. It also stores an LLM summary of what critics and players like and dislike, and links similar games from the catalog. A web UI lists the games, shows each game's card, and monitors the crawler live. Data comes from Metacritic's JSON backend, not HTML scraping. See [docs/metacritic-api.md](docs/metacritic-api.md). ## Architecture ```mermaid flowchart LR scheduler["APScheduler
every 60 min"] --> crawler runnow["Run now
POST /api/runs"] --> crawler crawler["Crawler
(one run at a time)"] --> metacritic["Metacritic
JSON backend"] crawler --> llm["LLM provider
chat + embeddings"] llm --> ollama["Ollama or any
OpenAI-compatible API"] crawler --> db[("PostgreSQL
(SQLite locally)")] web["Web UI + API
FastAPI, Jinja2, htmx"] --> db ``` One FastAPI process holds both the web UI and the scheduler. A crawl run lists games, fetches each game's details and per-platform scores, summarizes its reviews, embeds it for similarity, and records progress and errors on its `crawl_runs` row. The monitor page reads that row. ## Demo walkthrough Needs Docker. With the bundled Ollama, give Docker at least 8 GB of memory, 12 GB to be safe. `gemma3:4b` on the CPU peaks near 7 GB. In an 8 GB Docker the kernel killed the model once during a 20-game run. The crawler retried the call, and the run still finished with no errors. **1. Start everything.** ```bash cp .env.example .env docker compose --profile ollama up --build ``` The first start downloads the Ollama image (about 3.8 GB) and the `gemma3:4b` and `nomic-embed-text` models (about 3.6 GB). The app waits until both models are ready, then applies database migrations and starts the first crawl. Ollama in Docker on a Mac runs on the CPU only. For faster summaries, use the Mac's own Ollama instead: run `ollama pull gemma3:4b && ollama pull nomic-embed-text`, set `LLM_BASE_URL=http://host.docker.internal:11434/v1` in `.env`, and start with `docker compose up --build` (no profile). A hosted API works the same way, using `LLM_BASE_URL`, `LLM_API_KEY`, `LLM_MODEL` and `EMBED_MODEL`. **2. Watch the first crawl.** Open . Run #1 started when the app booted. Every 3 seconds the panel shows its status, games processed (up to 20), the error count with the last errors, and when the next scheduled run is due. A 20-game run took about 6 minutes with Ollama running natively on a Mac, and about 19 minutes with the bundled CPU-only Ollama in Docker. A hosted API is faster still. **3. Browse the catalog.** Open . Today's 20 New Releases are listed. - Type in the search box: the list filters as you type. - Pick a platform: the badges switch to that platform's scores. - Sort by user score. - The URL keeps the filters, so you can share it. **4. Open a game card.** Click any game to see: - cover, developer and genres - Metascore and user score per platform - the video link and a link to the game on Metacritic - the description - what critics and players like and dislike - up to six similar games; click one to jump to its card **5. Run now.** On the monitor, press **Run now**. - Run #2 starts at once, and the button st
